# Why Tides Happen

Tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea, and they are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and, to a lesser extent, the Sun. The Moon's gravity tugs on the Earth's oceans, drawing water toward it and creating a bulge on the side of the planet facing the Moon. At the same time, the Earth itself is pulled slightly toward the Moon, leaving the water on the far side of the planet behind. This creates a second bulge on the opposite side of the Earth. As the planet rotates beneath these two bulges, most coastal areas experience two high tides and two low tides over the course of roughly twenty-four hours and fifty minutes.

The Sun also exerts a gravitational influence on the oceans, though its effect is only about half as strong as the Moon's because of its enormous distance from Earth. When the Sun and Moon line up with the Earth — during a new moon or a full moon — their gravitational forces combine to produce especially high and low tides known as spring tides. When the Sun and Moon are at right angles to each other relative to the Earth, their pulls partially cancel out, resulting in gentler tides called neap tides.

The exact shape and timing of tides at any given location are further influenced by the contours of the coastline, the depth of the ocean floor, and the shape of the basin in which the water sits. These factors can amplify or dampen the tidal effect, which is why some places experience dramatic tidal ranges while others see only modest changes. Ultimately, tides are a constant reminder that the Earth is not an isolated world but one deeply connected to the gravitational forces of its celestial neighbours.
